en: Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty;
recorded by his disciple Fashen.

The third part of the sixth preliminary section on the preparatory practices for the *dhyānapāramitā*, concerning the disciple’s consecration and re-examination, consists briefly of two points regarding the verification of the real and the unreal.
First, the actual demonstration for verifying whether [the teaching] is true or false;
second, the discernment of whether it is a māra or not a māra.
Regarding the first, the demonstration for verifying whether it is true or false:
If, within meditative concentration,
one gives rise to various wholesome roots of dhyāna,
among these there are both the genuine and the counterfeit.
One must not mistakenly give rise to acceptance or rejection.
Why is this? Because when one gives rise to the various dhyānas and samādhis, [one must remain free from such errors].
The mind does not discern them;
one may see demonic meditative states and mistake them for the arising of roots of goodness.
The mind gives rise to grasping and attachment;
because of this perversion,
one falls ill and goes mad.
If it is a root of goodness,
one should recognize it as being fixed by Māra,
and with a mind of doubt, abandon it.
One immediately falls away from wholesome benefits;
this matter is difficult to discern.
If one wishes to know it specifically:
One should verify it by means of two methods;
thus one will know whether it is genuine or false.
First, one knows it through the examination of its characteristics.
Second, knowing through the verification of dharmas.
Regarding the first, knowing through the verification of characteristics,
there are two meanings.
First, the heterodox;
second, the orthodox.
As for the heterodox:
Just as when various contacts arise within the fundamental dhyānas,
whichever single contact arises,
if there is any false dharma, [it is abandoned].
This is precisely the characteristic of the perverse.
Perverse phenomena are numerous;
for now, we shall discuss them in relation to a single instance of contact.
Briefly stated, ten pairs of false dharmas are set forth to clarify the characteristics of the false.
The first is the increase or decrease of the substance of contact.
Second, meditative absorption versus distraction;
third, emptiness versus existence;
fourth, clarity versus darkness.
5. Sorrow and joy;
6. Pain and pleasure;
7. Good and evil.
8. Folly and wisdom;
9. Bondage and liberation;
10. Strength and softness of mind.
These ten pairs clarify the characteristics of the erroneous;
they are all distinguished in terms of either excess or deficiency.
First, regarding the increase or decrease of the substance of contact:
For example, when movement is initiated by contact,
if the body moves or the hand is raised, the feet follow as well; yet to an outsider,
it may appear motionless, as if one were asleep.
Or, as if possessed by a spirit, the hands and body may twitch and move;
or, while sitting, one may see various extraordinary visions—
these are signs of increase.
"Diminution" refers to when, at the initial stage of movement,
whether upward or downward,
it has not yet reached the entire body.
Even as they gradually decay and perish,
one thereby loses all objective spheres;
while sitting, one feels desolate and forlorn.
One is unable to maintain the body;
this is a sign of decline.
Second is mental distraction.
As for meditative concentration (*samādhi*): when movement, contact, or arousal occurs,
both consciousness-mind and the body [are affected].
Bound by meditative concentration,
one does not attain mastery; or,
as a consequence of this, one may even enter into false concentration.
"Even until seven days have passed without emerging.
Regarding "disturbance":
it refers to the time when movement, contact, or arousal occurs.
The mind and mental factors are disordered and distracted,
clinging to objects without ceasing.
Third, there is emptiness within emptiness.
At the moment of its activation,
one perceives no body at all;
this is called the realization of the concentration on emptiness.
As for "existence," at the moment of stimulation,
one perceives the body as solid and rigid.
They are like wood or stone.
Fourth, regarding light and darkness:
as for "light," it refers to—
At the moment of its activation,
one perceives various external colors and lights,
even including the light of the sun, moon, and stars, as well as the various radiances of blue, yellow, red, and white.
As for "darkness":
at the moment of contact, the body and mind become shrouded in obscurity.
It is like entering a dark room.
Regarding the five types of sorrow and joy: as for sorrow—
At the moment of contact,
his mind becomes feverish and distressed;
he grows haggard and unhappy.
As for joy (*prīti*):
at the moment it is triggered,
the mind experiences great exultation.
The courageous and active cannot find peace for themselves.
Sixth, suffering and pleasure.
Regarding suffering:
At the moment of contact,
the body and mind experience pain and affliction everywhere;
this is what is meant by "pleasure."
At the moment of contact,
there is immense pleasure; one becomes greedily attached and deeply entangled.
Seventh, good and evil.
Regarding the good:
at the moment it is triggered, it...
To be mindful of external, scattered wholesome thoughts and reflections that destroy samādhi is what is called "evil."
At the moment of arousal,
various unwholesome states of mind such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) arise.
These are the eight types of delusion and wisdom.
When a fool is touched by these, their mind and consciousness become deluded and confused.
When a wise person encounters delusion, confusion, and perversion,
they trigger [awakening].
When the faculty of discernment gives rise to false perceptions,
it destroys samādhi and the liberation from the nine bonds.
As for "bondage," at the moment of contact and arousal,
the five hindrances and various afflictions obscure the mind-consciousness.

When those who have attained liberation experience the arousal [of such thoughts], they claim to have realized the concentrations of emptiness and signlessness, to have attained the Path and its fruits,
and to have severed the fetters and achieved emancipation;
thus, they give rise to the conceit of superiority.
The ten states of mind are strong or weak.
As for the strong ones:
at the time they are triggered, they...
Their minds are rigid and stubborn;
they cannot attain mastery over their coming and going,
being as difficult to transform as tiles or stones.
Not following the path of virtue;
as for those who are weak,
at the moment they are provoked.
The will is weak and easily corrupted,
just as soft mud cannot be fashioned into a vessel.
These twenty kinds of unwholesome contacts disturb the mind while sitting and destroy meditative concentration.
This causes the mind to become deviant;
this is the sign of the arising of wrong concentration.
Furthermore, there are twenty types of deviant dharmas.
Whatever arises, if one does not distinguish it from false and deceptive thoughts and instead gives rise to attachment,
one may consequently lose one's mind and become deranged.
Sometimes they sang and sometimes they wailed;
sometimes they laughed and sometimes they wept;
at other times they became frantic and wandered aimlessly.
At times they fall ill; at times they meet with death;
at times they seek to throw themselves from cliffs or leap into fire.
They hang themselves or commit suicide;
such obstacles and afflictions are not limited to these alone.
Furthermore, among the twenty kinds of wrong views:
Whenever one gives rise to even a single false dharma,
should it correspond to any of the ninety-six types of paths or the dharmas of ghosts and spirits— even a single such dharma—
and yet one fails to recognize it as such.
Immediately recollecting that path and practicing that dharma,
the spirits and deities enter into the attained state of dharma in accordance with one's mindfulness.
By means of this, one realizes the Dharma-gate of ghosts and spirits;
the ghosts augment one's power,
or cause one to enter various deep and heterodox meditative absorptions.
As well as wisdom and eloquence;
knowing the auspiciousness and misfortune of the world;
and possessing miraculous and extraordinary supernatural powers.
Manifesting rare and wondrous events to move the hearts of sentient beings,
they widely propagate false teachings.
Some commit great evils and destroy the roots of goodness in others;
others, though they perform good deeds,
do so with hypocrisy and impurity.
The people of the world lack wisdom;
seeing only those who appear extraordinary,
they claim them to be sages and saints, and thus believe in and submit to them with deep hearts.
However, his inner mind was perverted;
he devoted himself exclusively to demonic practices and constantly taught such demonic methods to others.
Therefore, those who practice based on such faith will break the right precepts, break the right view,
break proper decorum, and break pure livelihood.
At times they consume excrement and filth;
they go naked without shame;
and they show no reverence toward the Triple Gem, their parents, or their teachers.
Or they may destroy scriptures, images, stupas, and monasteries;
commit various heinous crimes;
and sever their roots of goodness.
They manifest signs of impartiality,
or they praise themselves by claiming their conduct is impartial;
therefore, regarding what is not the path—
Being without obstruction or hindrance,
they disparage others' cultivation of goodness,
claiming it is not the true path.
Some say there is neither cause nor effect;
others say there are false causes and false effects.
Thus, such erroneous doctrines proliferate in confusion.
They will destroy and disrupt the True Dharma;
those who hear and accept it will have their minds defiled by false teachings.
Having internally realized the various dharma-gates of the merits of wisdom, abandonment, and samādhi resulting from false dhyāna,
his eloquence was then inexhaustible.
Through his majestic power he transforms sentient beings;
thus he gains the benefits of renown, retinues,
offerings, prostrations, and praise.
Therefore, the scriptures of the ninety-six kinds of paths state:
"When one preaches the Dharma for others,
ghosts and spirits bestow their power."
Then all who hear it will believe and accept it without exception;
all who see it likewise.
All gave rise to love and respect;
because of such matters as these,
they became deeply attached in their hearts, unable to turn back.
Mistaken conduct and perversions are manifold and not of a single kind;
if one is thus, it should be known that such a person is far removed from the noble Dharma.
When the body perishes and life ends,
they fall into the three evil realms;
this matter is explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*.
If you wish to know the characteristics of ghosts and spirits,
you should seek out the scriptures of the ninety-six kinds of paths and carefully compare, categorize, and discern them.
The facts can thus be known.
It is asked:
What of those who practice evil in association with false dharmas?
The faults of the present are such that,
upon the end of this life,
one shall be reborn within the three evil realms.
As for those who practice goodness with a deceitful mind,
what are their faults in the present life,
and where will they be reborn after death?
The answer is:
Although this person performs good deeds of body and speech that resemble the Buddha-dharma, their understanding and mind are perverse.
If one does not realize that the arising of obstacles [prevents] the outflow-free [wisdom] of the three vehicles,
although one has not yet encountered the truth,
within this mind of inversion—
At times, they are also able to cause the Three Jewels to flourish and manifest, exhorting sentient beings to cultivate goodness;
when such a person’s life comes to an end, [they will be reborn in the heavens].
They will not necessarily fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts;
rather, according to the dharmas corresponding to the spirits and deities with whom they associate,
they will be reborn in the same place as those spirits and deities.
They will again become members of those retinues,
or at times may be born among humans or devas;
thus it is said in the Sūtra of the Ninety-six Kinds of Paths.
There are more than sixty paths above;
because their perverse delusions and karmic obstacles are heavy,
it is necessary to recite mantras to treat them all.
Below these are twenty-odd paths;
those whose delusions and karmic obstructions are relatively light merely awaken to direct realization.
Furthermore, although such a person may be born among gods or humans,
they remain secretly and constantly bound to the path of Māra and heterodoxy,
delighting in associating with false teachers.
They delight in hearing false teachings,
delight in practicing false paths,
and make offerings to and draw near to them.
They praise and extol those who practice in deviant ways;
when they see those who correctly train in the three vehicles,
they take no pleasure in associating with them.
Or they may give rise to vexation and disturbance;
thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:
"Whether it be Māra or the sons of Māra..."
Whether it be māra-female spirits,
māra-subjects, or those possessed by māra,
the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra also says:
Whether they be celestial beings of Māra or humans of Māra,
one knows that such persons, though born among humans or devas,
still remain subject to Māra.
They constantly engage in demonic activities;
even after having left the household life,
they still continue to perform such deeds.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
the path of Māra will gradually arise."
Māra manifests as a bhikṣu to disrupt and confound the Buddha-dharma,
just as the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* extensively explains the characteristics of Māra’s activities.
This should be analyzed in detail therein;
just as it is with the false characteristics within a single instance of movement-contact,
so it is with the remaining seven types of contact.
These same signs of perversion are also present here;
they should be understood distinctly.
Just as the signs of perversion are in the fundamental dhyānas, so it is here.
The remaining fourteen gates concern dhyāna and all matters of both fact and principle within the various dhyānas.
All contain heterodox and false teachings;
their details are numerous and cannot be fully recounted.
Question: When one gives rise to wrong contact,
does one give rise to all twenty wrong things as described above?
"Is it that they are incomplete?
He replied,
"Whether they are complete or incomplete makes no difference."
If, when a [defilement] is triggered,
one does not immediately eliminate even a single unwholesome dharma, [it will persist].
One will thus fall into false certainty;
how much more so if one is fully possessed of twenty such false dharmas? Why is this so?
It is like twenty people traveling together;
if one among them is a thief, he endangers the other nineteen.
It is the same within dhyāna.
If there is a single unwholesome dharma that destroys all wholesome dharmas,
it cannot be called right concentration;
how much more so when there are many?
The brief exposition of the characteristics of the single contact is thus;
the same applies to the false characteristics of the remaining seven contacts.
Furthermore, there are other heterodox methods regarding the gates of dhyāna.
One should also recognize them while in meditative concentration;
that is to say, the objects of other dhyāna-gates which are false dharmas, such as,
for example, the dhyāna of the contemplation of impurity.
Upon entering this meditative absorption,
twenty false dharmas also arise; furthermore,
these enter this absorption through fourteen other gates of dhyāna.
It should also be understood in this way.
One should analyze each part individually;
herein, it should be explained in detail.
If a practitioner should attain realization of this dharma,
they must skillfully recognize it and clearly illuminate it through expedient means.
Not adhering to the dharmas of false concentration,
he immediately withdrew of his own accord.
Second, to clarify the characteristics of correctness:
When movement and contact arise,
one is not subject to the twenty unwholesome dharmas and is fully endowed with the ten wholesome dharmas.
There are ten kinds.
Regarding wholesome dharmas:
first, the characteristic of contact is in accordance with the Dharma.

Second, the characteristic of concentration is in accordance with the Dharma; third, the characteristic of emptiness is in accordance with the Dharma; fourth, the characteristic of luminosity is in accordance with the Dharma.
5. The aspect of joy is in accordance with the Dharma.
6. The aspect of pleasure is in accordance with the Dharma.
7. The aspect of the wholesome is in accordance with the Dharma.
The characteristics of the eight knowledges are in accordance with the Dharma; the characteristics of the nine liberations are in accordance with the Dharma;
the characteristics of the mind's pliancy are in accordance with the Dharma.
What is meant by "in accordance with the Dharma"?
It refers to that which is contrary to the twenty unwholesome characteristics of phenomena,
and is thus secure and pure.
Harmony and appropriateness are precisely what constitutes accordance with the Dharma;
this is termed the "correct characteristic."
This matter will be explained later in the seventh major section, which clarifies the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) of the fundamental first dhyāna; therein,
their characteristics shall be analyzed in detail,
such as the true characteristic of a single movement of contact.
The true characteristics of the remaining seven types of contact can be understood by analogy with this.
Question: In this context, why is it explained solely by following the specific instances?
If one discriminates according to these signs,
[judging] whether they are false or correct,
counterfeit or genuine, [one falls into error].
"This should be abandoned and this should be accepted;
is this not a perverted conception that falls into error?
He replied, "Correctness is of two kinds."
First is mundane correctness;
second is supramundane correctness.
If explained according to the characteristics of mundane wholesome dharmas:
This is explained as the true characteristic of the mundane;
it is explained as the true characteristic of the supramundane wholesome dharmas of liberation.
This is the true characteristic of the supramundane.
Now, to clarify the ten kinds of correct characteristics within fundamental contact (*mūla-sparśa*),
this is precisely the exposition of the correctness of the world (*loka-samyaktva*). As the Mahāyāna-śāstra says:
Based on mundane right view, one attains supramundane right view; if mundane right view is destroyed,
[supramundane right view is likewise lost].
This immediately destroys the supramundane right view.
Therefore, if one now wishes to clarify the supramundane Right Dharma,
it is essential first to clarify the mundane Right Dharma.
Since one desires to reveal the principle through phenomena and clarify the remote by means of the proximate,
it is necessary first to distinguish the primary characteristics of the initial contact within the fundamental phenomena.
Furthermore, when contact arises internally,
one may either perceive the thirty-six constituent substances,
or give rise to the causal conditions for the thought of loving-kindness, correct wisdom, mindfulness of the Buddha, and other various meditative concentrations.
If there is merit that is peaceful and in accordance with the Dharma,
providing nourishment and contact with pleasure,
this too is the manifestation of roots of goodness from past lives.
Each has ten kinds of correct signs, all of which constitute right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
However, for those who wish to cultivate and achieve the fundamental dhyāna-concentration:
In all cases, one must not grasp at these signs.
Whether the practitioner is thanked or not,
it does nothing to hinder their fundamental dhyāna.
However, practitioners in the final age possess meager roots of goodness;
at the time of realization and contact [with reality],...
Generally, other matters and principles do not manifest within the meditative states; however,
I now fear that if they were to manifest, one might fail to recognize them.
This general intent has been briefly set forth.
The remaining fourteen gateways of dhyāna that give rise to the correct signs should also be understood in this same way.
Each of these categories is analyzed in detail according to its own kind.
Second, regarding the discernment of the false and the correct through the examination of dharmas:
there are indeed false forms of dhyāna.
Its characteristics are subtle and difficult to distinguish;
they resemble those of true dhyāna,
yet they cannot be differentiated by means of signs alone.
One should verify this through three methods:
first, by refining with a concentrated mind;
second, by cultivating and treating it with the fundamental method.
Third is analytical discernment through wisdom,
as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"If one wishes to know true gold..."
One should test it in three ways:
by burning, cutting, and rubbing.
A practitioner, too, is difficult to distinguish.
If one wishes to distinguish them,
one must also test them in three ways;
that is to say, one should engage in joint activities with them.
One who does not know through shared work should be observed over a long period; one who does not know through long association should be observed even longer.
Observing with wisdom,
I shall now borrow this point to clarify the characteristics of correct and deviant meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
If, upon the arising of a single movement of contact,
one has not yet discerned whether it is erroneous or correct,
one should enter deeply into a concentrated mind.
Regarding the objects that arise,
one neither grasps nor rejects them,
but simply abides with a mind of equanimity and stability.
If these are roots of goodness,
as meditative concentration becomes increasingly profound,
the roots of goodness become increasingly manifest.
If it is the work of Māra, it will naturally perish before long.
Second, one should cultivate and rectify it by means of the fundamental method,
such as when developing the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
He returns to the practice of the contemplation on impurity;
as he practices, the object of his meditation becomes increasingly clear and vivid.
This is not false; if one cultivates and refines it according to its fundamental nature,
it will gradually be destroyed and extinguished.
One should know that this is precisely a false characteristic.
Third, as for "observing with wisdom," it refers to observing the phenomena that have been produced.
Investigating the source and origin,
one finds no place of arising;
one deeply realizes emptiness and stillness.
When the mind does not dwell in attachment,
the false will naturally extinguish itself and the correct will naturally manifest itself.
Just as when genuine gold is heated, its luster and color are enhanced,
whereas if it is counterfeit gold,
it turns black and deteriorates on its own.
Thus, by distinguishing them through examination with these three dharmas,
the false and the correct can be known;
meditative concentration is likened to a grindstone.
Cultivation and purification are like beating;
wisdom-observation is like burning with fire.
Furthermore, dwelling for a long time is likened to grinding;
engaging in joint activities is like striking;
and being burned by fire is an analogy for the observation of wisdom.
Examine other instances of meditative concentration (dhyāna) in this same manner;
then the false and the authentic can be discerned. Second, distinguishing between that which is demonic and that which is not demonic.
This constitutes two points:
first, clarifying the characteristics of Māra;
second, clarifying what are not the characteristics of Māra.
Now it is explained that there are two kinds of differences regarding demonic dhyāna (*mārādhyāna*).
First, it is explained that while the dhyāna itself is not demonic,
demons may enter into the dhyāna.
Just as a practitioner gives rise to various meditative absorptions within a state of right mind,
the evil Māra fears that his path will become exalted.
They cause disturbance and enter into his meditative absorption;
if the mind becomes greedily attached, [it is lost].
If one gives rise to anxiety or fear,
Māra will immediately find an opportunity; however,
if one can apply the mind as described above to repel it, [Māra will be thwarted].
Once the demonic and heterodox influences have been extinguished,
it is like the sun appearing when clouds are cleared away;
the concentrated mind becomes luminous and pure.
Second, it clarifies how Māra exclusively manifests as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to deceive and delude the practitioner;
if one recognizes this as not being genuine, [one is not deceived].
He governs them by means of the Dharma.
Once the Māras have retreated,
there is not even a hair’s breadth of Chan practice remaining.
Next, to clarify what constitutes a non-demonic sign:
when karmic obstructions affect meditative concentration,
they may appear to be the work of a māra, yet in reality, they are not a māra.
It is difficult to distinguish and identify.
Even if one employs the methods previously described to repel it,
it will ultimately not depart.
If one can diligently practice repentance,
once the offenses have been eliminated,
meditative concentration will naturally become clear and distinct.
Furthermore, at the time of entering meditative absorption,
if one's skillful means are unskillful,
it will cause the objective sphere to become improper.
If one further skillfully applies expedient means,
then because that which is realized is pure and clear,
one knows it is not the work of Māra.
Fourth: Next, to distinguish and clarify the indeterminate nature of the arousal of dhyāna,
it is briefly set forth in five points.
First, the correct discernment of the two cultivations of principle and phenomena regarding the arising of dhyāna, which is not fixed;
second, clarifying the causes and conditions for the arising of dhyāna;
third, distinguishing the quantity of the arising of dhyāna.
The fourth clarifies the signs of the exhaustion of previously cultivated roots of goodness;
the fifth distinguishes between those with outflows and those without outflows.
First, regarding the preliminary discernment of the two cultivations of phenomena and principle, which give rise to indeterminate dhyāna:
it is asked, "Regarding the three types of cessation (śamatha) explained above..."
If one conditions the mind through objects,
both of these forms of cessation are cessations of phenomena;
one should simply give rise to meditative concentration within phenomena.
Since the essence is truly one and quiescent,
and this is the cessation of principle,
it should give rise to meditative concentration within that principle.
Now, for what reason do the three types of cessation all give rise to the various meditations on both phenomena and principle?
In this case, cause and effect would be conflated without distinction.
The answer is: it is not so. Now, in our school, both phenomena and principle are cultivated together;
this is entirely in accordance with the faculties and conditions of the practitioner.
Therefore, the methods for generating the aspiration differ.
It is better to definitively establish the distinctions.
Regarding the three types of cessation explained above,
if they were to be stated briefly, it should be as you have asked.
Combined, these constitute the two types of cultivation:
that of phenomena and that of principle. If analyzed in full detail, they should be expanded into four types of cultivation.
Regarding the four types of cultivation,
there are two kinds: first,
explaining the four cultivations from the perspective of śamatha (calm abiding).
Second, the four types of cultivation are explained according to the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
First, regarding the explanation of the four types of cultivation according to the gate of tranquility (*śamatha*): first is the tranquility of the object (*vastu-śamatha*).
What is called "stopping through focusing on objects and restraining the mind" is the cultivation of phenomena (vastu-bhāvanā).
Second is stopping through principle (tattva-śamatha).
What is called "stopping by realizing the truth" (tǐzhēn zhǐ) is precisely cultivation according to principle (lǐxiū). This constitutes the third category:
stopping according to principle (lǐzhǐ).
What is called "stopping that takes the conventional as its object while its essence is true" is the cultivation of both phenomena and principle;
"stopping that is neither phenomenon nor principle" is the fourth.
This refers to the cessation that stills the conceptualization of the two extremes;
it is cultivation that is neither based on phenomena nor on principles.
Second, regarding the four modes of cultivation as explained through the gate of contemplation:
Contemplation of phenomena refers to practices such as the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) and the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*);
these constitute the cultivation of phenomena.
Second is contemplation of principle (*li-guan*),
namely the contemplation of emptiness, signlessness, and so forth;
this is cultivation of principle (*li-xiu*).
Third is the contemplation of both phenomena and principle,
which refers to the simultaneous contemplation of the two truths;
this is precisely the cultivation of phenomena and principle.
The fourth is neither the contemplation of phenomena nor the contemplation of principles; it is what is called the Middle Way’s correct contemplation.
This is precisely the cultivation that is neither of phenomena nor of principles.
Now, this is intended to establish the meaning of the indeterminate nature of dhyāna arising from the preceding gate of *śamatha*.
However, the practice is explained solely in terms of the four *śamatha* (calm abidings).
Within each of these practices,
there are four distinct ways in which the arising of dhyāna may be indeterminate.
Therefore, among the four types of cultivation,
there are collectively sixteen kinds of indeterminate arousal of dhyāna;
the practitioner should clearly recognize these signs.
One immediately realizes for oneself the dual cultivation of phenomena and principle,
which universally gives rise to all dhyānas and samādhis,
such that the mind is free from doubt or confusion.
Regarding what are called the four types of cessation (*śamatha*), each has four kinds of indeterminate arousal of dhyāna.
Now, first we shall examine the first matter: the indeterminate arousal of dhyāna through practice.
There are four distinct types [of practitioners].
First, there are those who practice by settling the mind,
fixing it on an object, and restraining the mind through such means as *śamatha*.
Furthermore, it refers to the meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi) within the context of the actual practice of cultivation, namely:

the four fundamental dhyānas, the four immeasurables (apramāṇa), the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti), as well as the nine notions of repulsiveness (aśubha-saṃjñā), the liberations (vimokṣa), the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana).
Second, there are practitioners who settle their minds in the practice of *śamatha*,
yet only give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) within the realm of principle.
This refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the various dhyānas and samādhis within the principles of wisdom-practice such as the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
and thirdly, those who personally practice these methods.
The matter of settling the mind ceases;
one fully develops the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of both phenomena and principle, namely:

the four fundamental dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and so forth.

The various dhyānas and samādhis within the wisdom-practice principles of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four noble truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and so forth—
even up to the *viśeṣa* and *abhijñā-vyakti*— all belong to the meditative concentrations of both phenomena and principle.
Fourth, there are practitioners who settle the mind in the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding),
thereby giving rise to a meditative concentration that is neither based on objects nor on principles.

This refers to the dhyānas and samādhis subsumed under the Middle Way, such as the dhyāna of intrinsic nature, all dhyānas, and others, including the Lotus Samādhi, the Single Practice Samādhi, the Śūraṅgama, and the Lion’s Roar.
Up to and including the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
It is asked: If one practices the cultivation of tranquility (śamatha), [how does one proceed]?
One should only give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) regarding phenomena (*vastu*).
How, then, can one now give rise to various dhyānas and samādhis concerning principles (*li*), non-phenomenal principles, and so forth—
the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*)?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of the arousal of dhyāna.
The first is that which is attained through the cultivation of present expedient means.
Second, it awakens the roots of goodness from past lives.
If one cultivates the dhyāna of phenomena and thereby awakens that dhyāna of phenomena,
it is mostly attained through cultivation.
If one cultivates phenomena and gives rise to the principle, or gives rise to that which is neither phenomenon nor principle, such as various dhyānas and samādhis,
all of these are the manifestation of the roots of goodness from meditative concentration cultivated in past lives.
This is like the Sāṃkhyas who distinguish two types of cultivation.
First, cultivation through acquisition; second, cultivation through practice.
Cultivation through acquisition refers to that which has not been previously attained.
The cultivation of practice is defined as that which has already been attained previously;
this category is likewise so.
Therefore, with respect to the cultivation of the actual phenomena (*vastu-bhāvanā*), there are four types of indeterminate [attainments] that give rise to dhyāna.

Furthermore, what is clarified here in this internal method (antara-upāya) merely distinguishes the causes for the cessation and arousal of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) from previous lives; therefore,
although it describes the signs of arousal regarding the various dhyānas and samādhis of both phenomena and principle, [it does not concern the present life].
All [of these] are brief and superficial.
If one were to discuss the cultivation and accomplishment [of the path],
the cause and its result would correspond [to one another].
From beginning to end,
the phenomena and principles of the various dhyānas and samādhis are vast, profound, and deep in their characteristics.
These all belong to the seventh major section,
wherein they are further analyzed in full detail.
It is asked:
If the various uncommon dharmas, such as the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and samādhis that arise from practicing specific matters rather than non-matters or non-principles,
are all obtained through causes and conditions cultivated in previous lives,
then one should practice everything in accordance with those specific matters.
All should have attained uncommon dharmas such as the Śūraṅgama and other various dhyāna-samādhis. If this is so,
for what reason do all the Buddhas of the ten directions earnestly praise the Prajñāpāramitā?
If one can act in accordance with what has been heard,
the practitioner will then be fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
He replied:
This objection further establishes the present point. Why is this?
If a practitioner has already encountered immeasurable Buddhas in the past.
From the presence of the Buddhas,
they hear the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā and practice it exactly as they have heard it.
Then, whatever one cultivates in this present life,
all non-essential and irrational dharmas of meditative concentration and samādhi that are not shared with others will spontaneously manifest.
If, in the past, one did not hear the Prajñāpāramitā and did not cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā,
then even if one hears it and cultivates it in this present life, one will be unable to give rise to it.
How much less could it arise for one who neither hears nor practices it?
Furthermore, although one may hear and practice the Prajñāpāramitā in this present life, it may not yet arise;
however, in a future life, if one encounters Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, [it will arise].
Upon hearing the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā,
one practices according to what has been heard;
this is the unique quality of all the meditative concentrations and samādhis of the Mahāyāna.
All shall be fully developed.
Therefore, know that these are all instances of hearing the Prajñāpāramitā and practicing according to what has been heard.
The ability to give rise [to this] is not without causes and conditions; for this reason,
all Buddhas of the ten directions earnestly praise the Prajñāpāramitā.
If there are those who practice according to what they have heard,
they will be able to fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas;
this correctly establishes the present meaning.
Furthermore, by virtue of the power of skillful means (*upāya*) in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
the practitioner is able, within the cultivation of phenomena (*vastu*),
to simultaneously possess the cultivation that is neither phenomenon nor principle (*avastu-anadharmabhāvanā*).
One who is courageous and diligent,
constantly practicing and cultivating,
will be able to give rise to all the uncommon dharmas of meditative concentrations and samādhis that are neither mundane affairs nor based on worldly principles.
Question: What is the difference between this and the previous [case]? Answer:
Within this, one should apply a fourfold analysis (catuṣkoṭi):
first, the cause is strong while the condition is weak;
second, the cause is weak while the condition is strong.
Third, both the cause and the condition are strong.
Fourth, both the cause and the condition are weak.
First, the cause is strong while the condition is weak.
It is able to give rise to various uncommon dharmas of dhyāna and samādhi that are neither mundane affairs nor based on worldly principles,
as analyzed previously.
Second, the causes are weak while the conditions are strong.
It is able to give rise to the uncommon dharmas of various dhyānas and samādhis that are neither mundane affairs nor [mere] principles;
this is precisely what is clarified here.
These three causal conditions are all powerful.
Regarding the ability to give rise to the uncommon dharmas of various dhyānas and samādhis that are neither mundane affairs nor worldly principles:
this refers to the aforementioned [past] being joined with the present;
this is precisely what constitutes those matters.
This person attains the most excellent Dharma.
If all four causal conditions are weak,
then in this present life, [the aspiration] may or may not arise.
Even if one were to attain the arising of dhyāna,
it would be feeble, shallow, and not stable.
In the final age, those who practice the highest path are most prone to falling away and losing their attainments.
It can only be thus.
As for what has been clarified in the three preceding lines,
perhaps one in ten thousand may possess it, or perhaps not even one.
The second type, the cultivation of dhyāna through the refinement of discernment,
is also indeterminate and likewise possesses four different varieties.
First, there are those practitioners who...
When the mind is at ease, one realizes the truth and comes to rest;
this in turn gives rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) within that truth,
namely all the various dhyānas and samādhis within such principles as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Second, there are practitioners who,
while establishing their minds in *śamatha*,
merely give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) within the midst of active phenomena.
This refers to the various dhyānas and samādhis within all matters that are turned away from by means of the fundamental dhyānas.
There are three types of practitioners:
those who settle their minds in the cessation of thought (śamatha).
Furthermore, they fully develop meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) regarding both phenomena and principle, namely:

the fundamental dhyānas, the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) concerning phenomena and principle, such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and so forth.
There are four types of practitioners.
With a mind settled in peace,
one then gives rise to meditative concentrations that are neither based on phenomena nor principles—
namely, the uncommon dharmas of all meditative absorptions and samādhis subsumed within the Middle Way, such as the dhyāna of intrinsic nature and so forth.
The various characteristics of the dhyānas are extensively analyzed,
as well as the categories of their cultivation and realization,
as explained in the first section.
The third matter, the cultivation and development of the indeterminate dhyāna through the discernment of principles,
also has four different types.
First, there are those practitioners who...
When the mind is settled and the conventional body rests upon the true reality of phenomena and principle,
one immediately returns to the meditative concentration of phenomena and principle—
namely, the fundamental dhyānas, the liberations (vimokṣa), emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), and all other meditative absorptions (samādhi) concerning both phenomena and principle.
Second, there are practitioners who settle their minds in the principles of phenomena and reality through *śamatha*,
yet only give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) within the midst of activities.
This refers to all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) within the various practices such as the fundamental dhyānas and the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Thirdly, there is the practitioner who settles the mind upon both phenomena and principle (*śamatha*).
However, one merely gives rise to meditative concentrations within the principle,
namely all the various dhyānas and samādhis within the principle such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and so forth. Fourth,
there are practitioners who proceed by themselves.
When the practice of calming the mind through phenomena and principle has ceased, one then gives rise to the meditative concentration that is neither phenomenon nor principle;
this refers to the uncommon dharmas of all meditations and samādhis subsumed under self-nature dhyāna and the Middle Way.
The various characteristics of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are extensively analyzed,
as well as the categories of their cultivation and realization,
as explained in the initial sections of the verses.
The fourth category, the indeterminate cultivation and realization of dhyāna that is neither based on the literal nor the rational,
also has four different types.
First, there are those practitioners who...
Settling the mind and breathing stills both extremes;
the cessation that is neither based on phenomena nor on principle gives rise in turn to a dhyāna that is neither based on phenomena nor on principle.
This refers to the unique dharmas of all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and samādhis, including the dhyāna of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-dhyāna*) and those subsumed under the Middle Way.
Second, there is the practitioner who settles the mind in *śamatha* (calm abiding), which is neither a matter nor a principle.
However, one merely gives rise to meditative concentrations within the midst of activities—
namely, all the dhyānas and samādhis within various activities, such as the eight fundamental dhyānas and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa).
There are three types of practitioners.
The settling of the mind is neither a matter nor a principle;
it is simply the arousal of meditative concentration within the realm of principle—
that is, all the various dhyānas and samādhis within the realm of principle, such as emptiness, signlessness, and so forth.
Fourth, there are practitioners who settle their minds in a state of cessation that is neither based on phenomena nor principles,
yet fully develop meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) regarding both phenomena and principles.
This refers to the fundamental dhyānas, the liberations (vimokṣas), and all meditative concentrations (samādhis) concerning the principles and phenomena of emptiness, signlessness, and so forth;
it provides a detailed analysis of the characteristics of these various dhyānas,
as well as a systematic examination of the categories of their cultivation and realization.
As explained in the first section,
here we shall distinguish only the four types of cultivation within the gate of *śamatha* (calm abiding).
Thus, there are sixteen kinds of indeterminate arousal of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
If one further distinguishes the four types of cultivation within the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*),
there are likewise sixteen kinds of indeterminate arousal of dhyāna; these are analyzed by combining both tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
There are thus thirty-two kinds of arousal;
the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are not fixed. These are the thirty-two.
This is based solely on the classification of those who practice through the Dharma (dharmānusārin). As for those who practice through faith (śraddhānusārin),
it is not fixed that they will attain awakening through dhyāna upon hearing the teachings on the gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
There are also thirty-two kinds;
their details are as follows,
but they are not fully set forth here.
This is a general discussion presented in brief as sixty-four types;
if one were to provide a detailed analysis according to the faculties and natures of persons belonging to the three vehicles, [the number would be far greater].
Thus, there are one hundred and ninety-two varieties of differences in the arousal of dhyāna.
If one were to examine these dhyānas in detail,
as well as distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
If one were to distinguish the various manifestations of their arising,
they would be immeasurable; however,
what is presented here is entirely a classification according to the mental states and stages of practitioners.
This is no empty or fabricated statement.
You should know that the methods for eliciting meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) are inconceivable;
they are the realm of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It is not even measurable by those of the Two Vehicles;
how could it be fathomed by ordinary beings?
If a practitioner wishes to cultivate themselves and transform others, [they must rely on this].
One must at least have some partial understanding of it;
it is better to err than to follow one's own heart, for that leads to the faults of harming oneself and others.
That which one has cultivated and refined is devoid of wisdom and benefit.
Second, this clarifies the source from which various dhyānas and samādhis arise.
There are two different interpretations regarding this.
First, some masters say that one should simply cultivate the higher entry into meditative concentration.
The various dhyānas arise spontaneously without requiring further cultivation;
this master exclusively employs the method of śamatha (calm abiding) throughout.
Regarding the instruction on treating people and so forth:
former physicians used medicinal milk exclusively;
now we do not follow this practice.
The reason for this is that cessation is a single dharma; therefore,
the dharma of origination should likewise be only one.
Since the meditations developed through the practice of both "calming" (śamatha) and "insight" (vipaśyanā) differ,
how can one claim that [liberation] arises solely from calming?
This not only constitutes an error regarding the principle.
This also deviates from the gateway of the Buddha's teachings.
Second, some teachers say that he practiced various meditative concentrations (dhyāna) throughout his past lives.
With roots of goodness as the cause,
one cultivates tranquility (śamatha) in this present life,
taking the attainment of meditative concentration (samādhi) as the condition.
Therefore, it can be seen that their arising is distinct and not identical.
For example, although there are various kinds of medicinal herbs, trees, and forests on dry land, they differ in species.
Names and forms are each distinct.
If they were not equally moistened by the rain of a single flavor,
how could there be such differences in their growth as various species?
This is also like that.
If one relies on the Mahāyāna interpretation regarding the seven treasures within the dark room, the jars, the basins,
and the well, this is a distinct discussion.
Third, regarding the extent of the methods for generating [samādhi]:
although it was previously established that the causes for cessation apply universally to the generation of all dhyānas and samādhis,
the faculties and natures of practitioners differ.
There are differences in the extent to which one may resolve to practice the Dharma.
Some individuals resolve to practice only a single type of meditative gate (*dhyāna-mukha*),
while others resolve to practice two, three, four, or five gates.
There may be a person who simultaneously activates all fifteen gates as well as all dhyānas and samādhis;
it cannot be definitively determined.
This is because such is the case:
all of this arises from the differences in the past habitual causes of the practitioner— whether they were partial or complete, and whether they were thick or thin—
as well as from their diligence or indolence in the present life.
Because there is a distinction between those who possess wisdom-convenience (*prajñopāya*) and those who lack wisdom-convenience,
the excellence or inferiority of their realization of the Dharma differs accordingly.
The divergence of paths and the differences among the myriad categories thus briefly clarify the characteristics of the varying degrees of the arousal of the dharma.
Fourth, clarifying the meditation that arises from cessation.
There are those that are exhaustive and those that are not.
For now, I shall clarify this by means of what is easily manifest;
therefore, I will first differentiate it within the context of a single meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
There are practitioners who,
having already cultivated this in previous lives,
have attained the visualization of impure bones emitting light.
Now, within this state of cessation, one has merely produced the perception of impurity but has not yet attained the flowing radiance of white bones;
this is called "incomplete."
If it is fully developed,
it is called "exhausted.
If it is that which was practiced in the past...
When the momentum is exhausted,
even if one continues to practice cessation (śamatha),
there will be no further progress.
If one further concentrates the mind to clearly contemplate the white bones and refines the visualization of the skeletal person,
practicing with unremitting diligence, one will then become aware.
In accordance with what the mind contemplates,
the objects of perception gradually unfold and develop,
resulting in the eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ).
The practices of contemplation, training, perfuming,
and cultivation are all fully perfected;
this is precisely what is accomplished through skillful and diligent practice in the present life.
This is not related to the wholesome arising of past habitual causes. Question:
If the cultivation of the object of *śamatha* does not progress, why must it necessarily be due to the exhaustion of past habitual causes?
Alternatively, because they are obstructed by karmic hindrances from past lives,
their former roots of goodness cannot increase or be brought to fruition.
The answer is:
It is indeed as the Tathāgata has asked;
this distinction is one path that is not obstructive,
for there are those who naturally bring it to full completion.
This does not concern karmic obstacles;
one must necessarily practice by relying on skillful means according to the method of contemplation,
and only then will accomplishment be attained.
Within this, one should examine and distinguish five types of individuals according to their spiritual faculties:
first, those of the nature of retrogression;
second, those of the nature of preservation.
1. Those who abide in the stage of penetration; 2. Those who progress toward penetration; 3. Those who have reached penetration; 4. Those who progress toward penetration;
5. Those who have reached penetration.
The detailed classifications and so forth are not recorded here in full.
The remaining fourteen dhyānas can be understood as being similar in their characteristics regarding whether they are fully developed or not.
Fifth, regarding the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Question: Above, the characteristics of the arising of the various dhyānas and samādhis were explained through fifteen gates.
Within this, there are both out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*);
as for out-flowing wholesome [dharmas],
they have been obtained through past experience.
If there could be a wholesome arising from a cultivated cause,
yet the untainted (anāsrava) has never before been attained,
how could there be a wholesome arising from a past cultivated cause?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of untainted [dharmas].
The first is the untainted [dharmas] of active practice.
Second, the practice of wisdom is untainted and the practice of conduct is untainted;
since these are both phenomena that serve as antidotes.
Not relying on conditions as ultimate reality,
one may obtain the past causes of habitual cultivation that are wholesome; thus, wisdom is generated and conduct becomes non-existent [in terms of grasping].
Since outflows (āsrava) are definitively dependent upon conditions,
it cannot be determined that there exists a past habitual cause for wholesome [states]; thus,
the practice of wisdom does not arise.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of outflows:
first, those cultivated by taking principle as the object,
practicing with clear wisdom.
Practicing the two [aspects] means generating wisdom to perceive principles and taking the truth as an object;
one practices by means of clear wisdom,
taking those principles as the object of cultivation.
Then there is the cultivation of causes that give rise to goodness;
wisdom arises and one perceives the principle. Although this still takes the truth as its object, it is nevertheless so.
Thus, there is no cause for habitual practice, and one skillfully brings forth [insight];
having brought it forth, wisdom perceives the truth.
Furthermore, there are two kinds.
First, the arousal of semblance wisdom;
second, the arousal of true wisdom.
[Regarding] the arousal of semblance wisdom:
There may be those who, through the cultivation of causes, skillfully give rise to the awakening of true wisdom;
yet there are those who, lacking the cultivation of causes,
do not skillfully give rise to the awakening of true wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the outflow-free [wisdom] of the vision of the truths, such as the patience regarding suffering;
second, the outflow-free [wisdom] of the cultivation of the three realms, such as the unhindered knowledges and liberations.
If one gives rise to the uncontaminated [wisdom] of the vision of the truths, such as the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*),
it is exclusively not considered to be produced by a cultivated cause; however, if one gives rise to the uncontaminated [wisdom] of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), [it is so considered].
Thus, the gates of the teaching are not fixed.
If one follows the interpretation of the Sarvāstivāda, the meaning is that the *srotāpanna*,
*sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat* may all fall away from their attainments.
When one returns from the first fruit and subsequently realizes a further fruit,
there is the arising of the wholesome cause of practice.
If one is a person of the three fruits who is of the non-retrogressive type, since there is no principle of re-arising,
it cannot be determined that they possess the wholesome arising of a habitual cause.
If one follows the interpretation of the Dharmaguptaka school regarding what is clarified by their intent,
the four fruits that give rise to true outflow-free wisdom all lack the cultivation-cause of wholesome arising.
Question: According to the analysis in the Abhidharma,
it is only the first arising of the outflow-free [state] that [is so].
There is no cause consisting of its own seeds;
how then can it be maintained that all true untainted states produced by the four fruits are exclusively without a cultivated cause?
[In response: It is because they are wholesome and produced through cultivation.
It is said: "Now, the meaning of the causal conditions for the arising and cultivation of the various dhyānas and samādhis is explained;
their underlying intentions are not the same."
The basis for this is that wholesome roots acquired in past lives were lost during the intervening period.
Now, based on cessation, further development occurs;
through the cultivation of causes, wholesome development arises,
and the four fruits bring forth true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*).
There are no causes for the loss or regression of what was previously attained through the sutras;
now, by practicing *śamatha*,
it is re-awakened.
How could they be considered analogous?
If one discusses the mind of the first stage in general— namely, the untainted true understanding—
it constitutes two types.
The untainted mental states of the nine grades function as such types [of causes]. Thus,
up to the ninth grade, it is by reference to these that the wholesome nature of the "cause of cultivation" (*abhyāsa-hetu*) is explained.
Thus, the untainted [states] produced by the four fruits are all termed "the arising of wholesome through the cause of practice.
Now, since this is not being explained in terms of the cause of practice, [it is not applicable here].
Therefore, it is said that those produced by the four fruits are all not produced by roots of goodness that serve as causes through habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*).
Furthermore, regarding the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and samādhis concerning both phenomena and principle that a practitioner cultivated in the past:
Although they have not yet attained realization or accomplishment,
they have already cultivated the roots of goodness of this life until they are now ripe;
they rely upon the cultivation of calm abiding as their condition.
All were fully opened and blossomed;
this was also the manifestation of the roots of goodness from their prior practice.
They were like those whom the Buddha had summoned with the words "Come, well-come," who were free from outflows.
He immediately gave rise to the three types of clear knowledge and the eight liberations,
possessing them all at once;
he then discerned that which is both with outflows and without outflows.
This continues up to "neither with outflows nor without outflows";
other categories may be understood by analogy.
